lessonTitle: Energy Release Rate and the Fracture Criterion

blocks.text: A 4 mm fatigue crack is found in a steel landing-gear forging that has already survived thousands of landings. Nothing about the crack has changed since yesterday, yet there is a particular stress at which it will suddenly run. Energy, not just stress, tells us where that threshold is.

blocks.markdown: A crack grows only if doing so lowers the total energy of the system, or at least does not raise it. Extending the crack by $\mathrm{d}a$ releases some stored elastic strain energy from the body, and costs energy to create the two new crack surfaces (plus any plastic work at the tip). Fracture happens when the energy released is enough to pay for the energy consumed. This is the energy balance idea of Griffith.

blocks.title: Energy release rate G
blocks.text: $G$ is the elastic energy released per unit of new crack area as the crack extends. Per unit thickness of a through crack, it has units of $\text{J/m}^2$, equal to $\text{N/m}$. The crack grows when $G$ reaches the material's critical value $G_c$, the energy it takes to create new fracture surface.

blocks.caption: Central crack of half-length $a$ in an infinite plate (Y = 1); $E'$ is the effective modulus defined below.

blocks.markdown: Compare this with $K = \sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$. Squaring gives $K^2 = \pi\sigma^2 a$, so the two are directly linked: $G = K^2/E'$. The stress intensity factor describes the crack-tip field while $G$ is the energy view of the same state. The effective modulus depends on constraint.

blocks.caption: $E$ = Young's modulus (Pa), $\nu$ = Poisson's ratio. For a given $K$ the plane-strain $G$ is slightly smaller because the thickness constraint stiffens the body.
Plane strain energy release rate for Mode I.

blocks.title: Energy release rate from K under plane strain
blocks.prompt: A thick section of steel ($E = 205$ GPa, $\nu = 0.3$, typical values) has $K_I = 35$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Find $G$ in $\text{J/m}^2$.

blocks.title: Fracture criterion
blocks.text: Unstable growth starts when $K_I$ reaches the material's critical value, $K_I = K_c$ (or $K_{Ic}$ for plane strain). Equivalently $G = G_c$. Rearranging for a through crack gives the critical stress and the critical crack length.

blocks.caption: Critical stress for a given crack, and critical crack length for a given stress.

blocks.title: Critical stress and critical crack length
blocks.prompt: A steel has $K_{Ic} = 60$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ (typical for a high-strength steel). A central crack of half-length 5 mm sits in a wide plate ($Y=1$). (a) Find the critical stress. (b) If the plate instead carries 250 MPa, find the critical half-length.

steps.text: Check the direction: the higher the stress, the smaller the crack that is tolerable. A crack 5 mm long is below the 18.3 mm limit at 250 MPa, so it is safe against fracture at that stress.

items: Stress doubled: the critical crack length drops to one quarter, since $a_c \propto 1/\sigma^2$.
Tougher material: $a_c \propto K_c^2$, so doubling toughness gives four times the tolerable crack.
Larger $Y$ (edge crack): both critical stress and critical length are lowered.

blocks.title: Half-length versus total length
blocks.text: In $K = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ the symbol $a$ is the half-length of a central crack. Always state whether a computed $a_c$ is a half-length (central) or a depth (edge) before comparing it with inspection data.

points: $G = K^2/E'$ with $E' = E/(1-\nu^2)$ in plane strain and $E$ in plane stress; $G$ is in J/m$^2$.
Fracture occurs when $K = K_c$ ($K_{Ic}$ in plane strain), so $\sigma_c = K_c/(Y\sqrt{\pi a})$.
The critical crack length is $a_c = (1/\pi)(K_c/(Y\sigma))^2$ and shrinks quickly as stress rises.

questions.stem: What are the SI units of the energy release rate $G$?

distractorRationale.a: That is the unit of K, not G.
distractorRationale.b: That is energy density, not energy per crack area.
distractorRationale.c: A force alone does not capture energy per area.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: energy per unit new crack area.

questions.explanation: $G$ is the elastic energy released per unit of crack area created, so its unit is joules per square metre, which equals newtons per metre. The unit MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ belongs to $K$, and the two are linked through $G=K^2/E'$.

questions.stem: A plate with a central crack is loaded to a stress at which it just fractures. If the crack had been twice as long (same geometry factor, same material), how would the critical stress change?

options.text: It would fall by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$

questions.correctOptionText: It would fall by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$

distractorRationale.b: Longer cracks always lower the critical stress.

questions.explanation: Since $\sigma_c = K_c/(Y\sqrt{\pi a})$, the critical stress varies as $a^{-1/2}$. A crack twice as long therefore lowers the critical stress by $\sqrt{2}$, about 29 percent.

questions.stem: For the same applied $K_I$ in the same steel, how does the plane-strain energy release rate compare with the plane-stress value?

distractorRationale.a: The factor $(1-\nu^2)$ is below one, so it reduces $G$.

questions.explanation: Plane strain constrains through-thickness contraction and stiffens the body, giving $E' = E/(1-\nu^2)$. Because $1-\nu^2<1$, $G=K^2/E'$ is smaller than the plane-stress value $K^2/E$.

questions.stem: A structure operates at a stress that is raised to 2 times its previous value. By what factor does the critical crack length (for the same material and geometry) change?

distractorRationale.c: Higher stress cannot raise the tolerable size.

questions.explanation: From $a_c = (1/\pi)(K_c/(Y\sigma))^2$ the critical length scales as $\sigma^{-2}$. Doubling the stress reduces the tolerable crack to a quarter.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the Griffith energy criterion for a growing crack?

options.text: The crack extends when the remote stress equals the yield strength
The crack extends when the energy released per unit crack area equals or exceeds the energy needed to create that area
The crack extends when the crack length equals the plate width
The crack extends when the strain energy stored becomes zero

questions.correctOptionText: The crack extends when the energy released per unit crack area equals or exceeds the energy needed to create that area

distractorRationale.a: Yield strength is not the fracture criterion.
distractorRationale.c: Width plays no role in the basic criterion.
distractorRationale.d: Stored energy does not need to vanish.

questions.explanation: Griffith balanced elastic energy release against the energy to form new surfaces. When $G$ reaches $G_c$, which is equivalent to $K=K_c$, growth is energetically favourable and, if $G$ increases with length, becomes unstable.

questions.stem: A thick aluminium component ($E = 70$ GPa, $\nu = 0.33$, typical) has a crack with $K_I = 20$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Find the plane-strain energy release rate $G$ in J/m$^2$.
questions.explanation: Here $G = K^2(1-\nu^2)/E = (2\times10^{7})^2(1-0.1089)/(7\times10^{10})$. This gives $5092$ J/m$^2$. Converting K to Pa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ before squaring is essential.

questions.stem: A single edge crack of depth 4 mm is in a wide plate of a steel with $K_{Ic} = 45$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Taking $Y = 1.12$, find the critical remote stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: $\sigma_c = K_{Ic}/(Y\sqrt{\pi a}) = 45/(1.12\times\sqrt{\pi\times0.004}) = 45/(1.12\times0.1121) = 358$ MPa. Using $K_{Ic}$ rather than $K$ makes this the fracture stress.

questions.stem: A wide plate (central crack, $Y=1$) of a material with $K_c = 50$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ carries a steady remote stress of 180 MPa. What is the critical crack half-length in mm?
questions.explanation: $a_c = (1/\pi)(50/180)^2 = 0.02456$ m, or $24.6$ mm. Because this is a central crack, the result is the half-length, so the total critical crack length is twice that.

questions.stem: Starting from the energy balance idea, explain why the relation $G = K^2/E'$ connects the energy and stress-field views of fracture, and state how $E'$ differs between plane stress and plane strain.
markingGuide: States that $G$ is the energy released per unit new crack area and $K$ scales the crack-tip stress field
Gives $G = K^2/E'$ and notes it follows from $G=\pi\sigma^2 a/E'$ with $K=\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$
Gives $E'=E/(1-\nu^2)$ for plane strain, and says why constraint stiffens the response
questions.explanation: Both $K$ and $G$ describe the same crack-tip state: $K$ the field amplitude and $G$ the energy supply. They are related by $G=K^2/E'$, where $E'$ depends on constraint, equal to $E$ in plane stress and $E/(1-\nu^2)$ in plane strain.

questions.stem: A wide plate (central crack, $Y=1$) of steel with $K_c = 40$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ carries 200 MPa. Inspection finds a crack of total length 12 mm. (a) Compute the critical half-length. (b) Decide whether fast fracture is expected and say what other failure mechanism could still make this crack dangerous.
markingGuide: Compares the measured half-length of 6 mm to the critical value and concludes fast fracture is not expected at 200 MPa
Notes fatigue or other subcritical growth could still enlarge the crack toward the critical size
questions.explanation: Using $a_c=(1/\pi)(40/200)^2=0.01273$ m, the critical half-length is 12.7 mm. The measured half-length is 6 mm, which is much smaller, so unstable fracture is not expected at this stress, but sub-critical growth by fatigue could eventually close the gap.
